paragraphs: A new law about Irish soldiers passed its first vote in the Dáil. 79 TDs voted yes and 71 voted no.
The law is about the Triple Lock. This is an old rule. It says when Ireland can send more than 12 soldiers to other countries.
Now three groups must say yes. They are the Government, the Dáil and the United Nations, or UN.
The Government wants to stop the UN part. Five big countries can block any UN plan. Defence Minister Helen McEntee says Ireland should make its own choices.
Many opposition TDs are angry. They held signs that said "save neutrality". They want the people to vote on the change.
The Government says no to a public vote. The law must still pass more votes. It could become law before the end of 2026.
A Government plan to change how Ireland sends soldiers abroad has passed its first vote in the Dáil. The bill won the support of 79 TDs, while 71 voted against it.

The plan would end the Triple Lock. This rule began in 1960, five years after Ireland joined the United Nations. It says that more than 12 Irish soldiers can only go on a mission abroad if three groups agree: the Government, the Dáil and the UN.

In practice, the UN part is the most important, because the Government usually controls the Dáil. But five countries on the UN Security Council, the US, Russia, China, Britain and France, can each stop a mission with a veto.

Defence Minister Helen McEntee says the Government wants to "fix what is broken". She believes Irish leaders, not other countries, should decide where Irish troops go. She gave the example of Irish soldiers who had to leave Lebanon after many years.

Opposition TDs strongly disagree. Some held up pages saying "save neutrality". Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said neutrality is linked to Irish values. Taoiseach Micheál Martin answered that the world has changed.

Many people want a referendum on the change, but the minister says no. The bill must now pass more stages in the Dáil and the Seanad. Then President Catherine Connolly, who once supported the Triple Lock, must sign it. The Government hopes it will become law before the end of 2026.
Legislation to scrap the Triple Lock, the system that controls when Irish troops can serve overseas, has cleared its first hurdle in the Dáil. The bill passed by 79 votes to 71 after a heated debate.

The Triple Lock dates back to 1960, five years after Ireland joined the United Nations. Under the rule, no more than 12 troops can be deployed on an overseas mission without approval from the Government, the Dáil and the UN.

Because the Government normally has a Dáil majority, UN approval has become the key condition. The Government argues that this gives too much power to the five permanent members of the Security Council, each of which can veto a peacekeeping mission.

Defence Minister Helen McEntee says the aim is to "fix what is broken" and keep decisions about Irish soldiers in Irish hands. She pointed to Irish troops in Lebanon, who were forced to leave after decades because of decisions taken elsewhere.

Opponents see the move as a threat to Irish neutrality. Opposition TDs displayed signs reading "save neutrality", while Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said respect for international law protects against military adventures. Taoiseach Micheál Martin replied that peacekeeping remains one of Ireland's most important commitments.
Professor Ben Tonra of UCD said the real issue is trust over who decides where troops are sent. Senator Tom Clonan, a former army officer, accused the minister of spreading misinformation.

The Opposition has demanded a referendum, but Ms McEntee has rejected the idea. The bill now moves to committee stage and must also pass the Seanad before President Catherine Connolly can sign it. It is expected to become law before the end of 2026.

A contentious bill to abolish the Triple Lock, which governs the deployment of Irish troops abroad, has survived its first Dáil vote. Following a fractious debate, the legislation was carried by 79 votes to 71, with two Fianna Fáil backbenchers abstaining.

The mechanism originated in 1960 legislation, enacted five years after Ireland's admission to the United Nations. It stipulates that a contingent of more than 12 troops may only be dispatched on an active mission with the endorsement of the Government, the Dáil and the UN.

Since any government typically commands a Dáil majority, UN authorisation has effectively been the decisive safeguard. Ministers contend that this hands an undue say to the five permanent members of the Security Council, any one of which can veto a peacekeeping operation.

Defence Minister Helen McEntee insists the reform will "fix what is broken" and return control over deployments to Irish ministers. She cited the withdrawal of Irish peacekeepers from Lebanon, dictated by decisions made outside the State.

Critics regard the change as an erosion of neutrality. Opposition TDs brandished placards urging the Dáil to "save neutrality", while Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald argued that adherence to international law guards against military adventurism. Taoiseach Micheál Martin, reminded that he once championed the Triple Lock, countered that the world has fundamentally changed.
Senator Tom Clonan, a retired officer, accused the minister of misinformation, whereas Professor Ben Tonra of UCD dismissed calls for a referendum as using a "sledgehammer to crack a lentil".

The bill now proceeds to committee stage before returning to the Dáil and moving on to the Seanad. It is expected to be enacted by the end of 2026, once signed by President Catherine Connolly, herself a vocal advocate of the Triple Lock.

Legislation designed to dismantle the Triple Lock, the statutory framework governing overseas deployments of the Irish Defence Forces, has passed its first parliamentary test. The bill secured the support of 79 TDs, with 71 opposed, although two Fianna Fáil backbenchers notably declined to vote.

Established in 1960, the Triple Lock stipulates that any deployment of more than 12 troops on an active mission is contingent upon three approvals: a Government decision, a Dáil resolution and a United Nations mandate.

In practice, the first two conditions are largely indistinguishable, as governments almost invariably command a parliamentary majority. Consequently, UN authorisation has functioned as the substantive safeguard. The Government maintains, however, that this arrangement renders Irish policy vulnerable to the veto power held by each of the five permanent members of the Security Council.

Defence Minister Helen McEntee has framed the reform as an effort to "fix what is broken", arguing that sovereignty over such decisions should rest with Irish institutions. She cited the withdrawal of Irish peacekeepers from Lebanon, which was ultimately determined by actors outside the State.

Nevertheless, the proposal has provoked substantial opposition. Critics characterise it as an erosion of neutrality, and Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald contended that adherence to international law constitutes a bulwark against military adventurism. Taoiseach Micheál Martin, who previously described the mechanism as central to neutrality, responded that the geopolitical landscape has been transformed.

Academic opinion is divided. Professor Ben Tonra of UCD suggested that the fundamental issue is one of trust, whereas Senator Tom Clonan, a former officer, alleged that the public had been misinformed.

Although opposition parties have persistently demanded a referendum, the minister has rejected this, maintaining that constitutional change would impede Ireland's capacity to respond to evolving threats. Following committee stage and Seanad scrutiny, the bill will require the signature of President Catherine Connolly, and it is anticipated to be enacted before the end of 2026.
